newsitem.title: THAILAND: WEEKAHEAD-Thai stocks set to carve out more gains.
newsitem.headline: WEEKAHEAD-Thai stocks set to carve out more gains.

text.p: A buying spree on the Thai bourse is set to continue this week although investors will soon have to evaluate their purchases as they wait for the baht to stabilise, analysts said.
Analysts and traders were euphoric as they watched the Thai stock market, which was at eight-year lows, leap 130 points in three days in response to the baht's managed float on Wednesday.
Buy orders were still in place and share prices, which gained nearly 25 percent in the shortened four-day trading week, would continue to rise in the coming week, they said.
"There seems to be a little bit more momentum," said George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett. "Our view is that the main logjam has been removed."
He said a fair value for the market, which ended on Friday at 657.09 points, was around 700.

"But people will soon need to evaluate what they've bought," he said. "Up to now they have been buying anything because they were afraid to be left behind. They just placed orders to buy up to the 10 percent limit -- it's been totally indiscriminate."

The Stock Exchange of Thailand said on Friday it would widen the daily stock price trading limit for shares on the bourse to 30 percent above and below the previous day's close. The move will not take effect until August 1.

Last week's rally was driven by foreigners who approved of recent bold moves to boost the ailing Thai economy, including Wednesday's shock decision to scrap the baht's fixed peg to a basket of currencies.
The baht exchange rate against the dollar, which initially lost nearly 20 percent of its value, is now set daily against a weighted average of the previous day's trading levels.
"Foreign investors wanted clear policy directives," said David Riedel, vice president and head of Thai research for Salomon Brothers.
"If you look at the last 10 days since Thanong (Bidaya) came in as finance minister you had some pretty dramatic changes," he said. "So the market does deserve to go up."

Thanong was named to replace Amnuay Viravan in the top finance job on June 20 and quickly took action to boost an economy mired by slowing exports, a growing current account deficit and high interest rates.

One of his first moves, made to fend off disaster in the frail finance sector, was to suspend activities of 16 ailing finance firms and order them to merge with healthy ones. This was followed by the baht's managed float and a rise of nearly two percentage points in lending rates to prevent the currency's meltdown. Analysts hope the next step, once the baht stabilises, will be an easing of interest rates which are among the highest in the region. This is not likely to be possible for a few months at least, they said.
"Once things settle down we have to be rather discriminating," Morgan said.
"A lot depends on what happens in the money market. The focus of the next weeks will be the value of the baht, and at what point will it stabilise."
On Friday the baht was relatively steady, trading at 28.50/29.00 per dollar near the close in the domestic market compared with 28.20/28.70 early in the day.
In the offshore market, it was quoted at 28.70/29.00, little moved from starting levels.
Currency dealers and analysts said the baht's stability could be attributed to improved short-term money market liquidity ushered in by renewed foreign investment in the stock market.
But dealers said stock trading was still very thin, with investors who had been badly burned in the past few weeks staying firmly on the sidelines.
Analysts agreed the government needed to show clear signs of continuing to implement and follow-up on its tough new directives in order to keep confidence in the economy.
"We still need to see some structural changes," said Riedel. "Interest rates are key. The only reason to float the baht is to...give them flexibility in interest rates."
